genes/PSEPK/groEL/groEL-ai-review.yaml.description: GroEL (PP_1361) is the cytoplasmic group I chaperonin of Pseudomonas putida KT2440. Conserved GroEL domains and curated HAMAP assignment support ATP-dependent folding and refolding of non-native proteins with the GroES co-chaperonin. Two heptameric GroEL rings form a chamber in which GroES capping and ATP-driven conformational changes coordinate client encapsulation and release. KT2440 stress-expression studies place GroEL within a proteostasis response, while the detailed folding-cycle mechanism is inferred from experimentally characterized homologs; the target-specific client repertoire remains unresolved.

genes/PSEPK/groES/groES-ai-review.yaml.description: GroES (PP_1360) is the cytoplasmic Cpn10 co-chaperonin of Pseudomonas putida KT2440. Its conserved heptameric lid binds the GroEL ring and helps create an enclosed folding chamber, contributing to ATP-dependent protein folding by the assembled GroEL/GroES machinery. ATP turnover occurs in GroEL; GroES supplies the capping and allosteric cofactor function. Curated HAMAP function and GroES-specific domains support this role in KT2440, with detailed chamber dynamics inferred from characterized homologs.

review.summary: The earlier GroES azido-ATP labeling result was challenged by direct equilibrium-binding and calorimetric experiments.
review.reason: The 1993 E. coli photolabeling report (PMID:7901771) was challenged by direct equilibrium-binding and calorimetric counter-assays (PMID:7867782). Those results establish a problem with treating the E. coli co-chaperonin as an ATP-binding protein, but they do not by themselves exclude ATP affinity in every homolog. No Q88N56 binding assay or source-specific reconstruction establishing how the InterPro mapping inherited the disproven claim was located. Retain uncertainty for KT2440; the supported core is GroEL binding and folding-cofactor activity, not intrinsic ATP binding.

supported_by.supporting_text: Using rigorous physical methods, isothermal calorimetry and equilibrium binding, no interaction between GroES and nucleotides could be detected.

review.reason: HAMAP-curated target localization states cytoplasm. This is a conserved localization inference, not a target-resolved imaging experiment.

review.reason: GroES performs structural and cofactor work in chamber formation, directly contributing to folding with GroEL. HAMAP target function and conserved architecture support this role; stress induction alone would establish neither autonomous folding nor exact kinetics.

review.summary: GroES assists folding by binding the GroEL complex; ATP hydrolysis is performed by GroEL.

supported_by.supporting_text: GroES binds to the apical surface of the GroEL ring, thereby capping the opening of the GroEL channel.

review.reason: The current GO definition includes binding a protein or protein-containing complex to assist folding. GroES fits through binding and remodeling the GroEL chamber; the core synthesis explicitly records contribution to the ATP-dependent complex activity and does not assert an autonomous ATP-powered GroES foldase.

review.summary: GroES-family metal binding has positive mycobacterial evidence, but its transfer to this target remains unresolved.
review.reason: PMID:11477217 demonstrates cation-dependent, EDTA-reversible changes in the Mycobacterium tuberculosis Cpn10 dome loop, and PMID:11807250 identifies metal-binding sites in that loop. The PTHR10772 PAINT assertion GO:0046872 at PTN000080668 is an ancestral judgment, not a pairwise transfer invalidated by a short donor list. No target-specific loss or counter-assay was found. Absence of a curated metal site in this target record cannot establish absence of binding; conversely the exact coordination-site conservation and target affinity have not been established here. Keep the claim unresolved rather than assert it as a core function or reject it.

supported_by.supporting_text: The binding sites for metal ions in the dome loop of cpn10 have been identified, suggesting the role of metal ions in the stabilization of the protein.
